title: Find the host that ran hot
briefing: Level 5 proved which rows of `metrics/node_metrics.csv` have the wrong shape. Now do the arithmetic the on-call engineer needed at 02:40: which host pegged its CPU, for how long, and how hard.
Two rows have the right shape but the wrong content. If you let them into the sums, your numbers will be wrong and nothing will tell you.

lesson.p: An awk array is indexed by any string, so `n[$2]++` keeps one counter per host without declaring anything. Build the arrays line by line, then print them in an `END` block with `for (key in array)`.

flags: count lines per value of field 2. A new key starts at 0.
for (h in n) print h, n[h]
loop over the keys in END. The order is not defined, so pipe the output through `sort`.
average = total / count. Divide only in END, when both are complete.
true only when field 3 is a number: `N/A` and `cpu` fail it

lesson.note: awk compares two values as numbers only when both look numeric. `N/A` and `cpu` do not, so `$3 > 85` becomes a TEXT comparison, and `"N/A" > "85"` is true because the character N sorts after the character 8. In a sum, the same values count as 0. Filter non-numeric values out before you compare or add.
A collector restart can write the header again in the middle of the file. `NR > 1` skips only the first one.

examples.title: Rows per host
examples.command: awk -F, 'NR > 1 {n[$2]++} END {for (h in n) print h, n[h]}' training/metrics.csv | sort

stages.why: Skip the header, then add 1 to the counter for this row's host.

stages.code: END {for (h in n) print h, n[h]}
stages.why: After the last line, print every host and its count.
`for (h in n)` visits keys in no particular order.

examples.title: A naive average, and why it is wrong
examples.command: awk -F, 'NR > 1 {s[$2] += $3; n[$2]++} END {for (h in s) printf "%s %.1f\n", h, s[h] / n[h]}' training/metrics.csv | sort

stages.why: Average to one decimal. db-01 comes out at 32.0: its `N/A` row was added as 0 and counted as a reading.

examples.title: The same average without the N/A
examples.command: awk -F, 'NR > 1 && $3 != "N/A" {s[$2] += $3; n[$2]++} END {for (h in s) printf "%s %.1f\n", h, s[h] / n[h]}' training/metrics.csv | sort

stages.why: Leave the missing reading out of both the total and the count.
db-01 is now 48.0, the true mean of 44.0 and 52.0.

examples.title: Peak per host, with guards
examples.command: awk -F, 'NR > 1 && NF == 6 && $3 != "N/A" {if ($3 > max[$2]) max[$2] = $3} END {for (h in max) print h, max[h]}' training/metrics.csv | sort

stages.why: Only complete rows with a real value. The truncated web-01 row (40.0) is dropped.

Keep the largest value seen per host. A key that is not there yet reads as 0, so the first positive reading always wins. For values that can be negative, start from the first reading instead: `!($2 in max) || $3 > max[$2]`.
Both sides are numbers now, so this is a numeric comparison.

challenge.question: Exactly one host in metrics/node_metrics.csv ever reported CPU above 85. Counting only rows whose cpu value is a number, which host is it, how many samples above 85 did it report, and what is the average CPU of those samples, to one decimal place?
challenge.format: Host, count, and average separated by single spaces, for example web-09 12 91.3

hints: Group by host (field 2), keep only samples above 85, and track a count and a total for each host. Then check what else slipped through: the header line, and anything in field 3 that is not a number.
`$3 + 0 == $3` is true only for numeric values. Combine it with `$3 > 85`, then `n[$2]++; s[$2] += $3`, and print `h, n[h], s[h] / n[h]` with `printf "%s %d %.1f\n"` in END.
awk -F, '$3 + 0 == $3 && $3 > 85 {n[$2]++; s[$2] += $3} END {for (h in n) printf "%s %d %.1f\n", h, n[h], ___}' metrics/node_metrics.csv

debrief.solution: awk -F, '$3 + 0 == $3 && $3 > 85 {n[$2]++; s[$2] += $3} END {for (h in n) printf "%s %d %.1f\n", h, n[h], s[h] / n[h]}' metrics/node_metrics.csv
debrief.alternative: awk -F, '$3 ~ /^[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?$/ && $3 > 85 {n[$2]++; s[$2] += $3} END {for (h in n) printf "%s %d %.1f\n", h, n[h], s[h] / n[h]}' metrics/node_metrics.csv
why: Without the numeric guard, the same program prints two lines: `host 2 0.0`, because both header lines (line 1, and line 1085 after a collector restart) pass `"cpu" > "85"` as text; and `bastion-7 29 90.4`, because the `N/A` sample at 23:45 passes as text and then adds 0 to the sum. Both errors are silent, and the second one looks plausible.

bastion-7 is a jump host. Its normal CPU is in single digits, so 28 five-minute samples at about 94% (23:25 to 01:40) is a miner or a busy exfil job, not a load spike. The window matches the sudo shell from Level 3.

On a real RHEL host, `sar -u -f /var/log/sa/saDD` gives the same history per day, and Performance Co-Pilot or node_exporter keep it for the whole fleet. Whatever the source, check the shape (Level 5) and the content (this level) before you put a number in a report.
